question.text: Suppose that \[ S = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n = 1}^\infty {\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^n}}}{{{n^2}}}} \] and that $s_6$ is the sixth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-s_6| < k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
Let $a_n = \dfrac{1}{n^2}$ and $b_n= {\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^n}}}{{{n^2}}}}.$ Then $a_n$ is positive and decreasing for $n\geq 1,$ and $a_n \to0$ as $n\to\infty.$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $6$th partial sum, it states that

\[ |S - {s_6}| < |{b_7}| =\left| \dfrac{( - 1)^7}{7^2} \right| =\dfrac{{1}}{{49}} .\]

Therefore, $k=\dfrac{{1}}{{49}} .$

example.title: Finding the Alternating Series Error Bound for a Given Partial Sum

question.text:
Suppose that
\[
S = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n = 1}^\infty  {\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^n}}\,n!}{{(n+4)!}}}
\]
and that $s_6$ is the sixth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-s_6| <  k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$ Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let $a_n ={\dfrac{ n!}{{(n+4)!}}}$ and $b_n={\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^n}}\,n!}{{(n+4)!}}}.$ Then $a_n$ is positive and decreasing for $n\geq 1,$ and $a_n \to0$ as $n\to\infty.$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $6$th partial sum, it states that

\[ |S - {s_6}| < |{b_7}| =\left| {\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^7}}\,7!}{{(7+4)!}}} \right| =\dfrac{{7!}}{{11!}} =\dfrac{1}{8\cdot 9\cdot 10\cdot 11}=\dfrac{1}{7920} .\]

Therefore, $k=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{7920}}.$

example.title: Finding the Alternating Series Error Bound for a Given Partial Sum

question.text:
Given that
\[
S = \displaystyle \sum_{n=2}^\infty \dfrac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{n(n^2+4)}
\]
and that $s_i$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that
$
|S-s_i| < 0.05.
$
question.explanation:
First, let \[ a_n=\dfrac{3}{n(n^2+4)} \quad\text{and}\quad b_n=\dfrac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{n(n^2+4)}. \] Then $a_n$ is decreasing for $n\geq 2$ and $a_n\to0$ as $n\to\infty.$ Therefore, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because the series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that \[ |S-s_i|<|b_{i+1}|. \]

Thus, we require \begin{align*} |b_{i+1}| = \left|\dfrac{3(-1)^{i+2}}{(i+1)\big((i+1)^2+4\big)}\right| &\le 0.05\\[5pt] \dfrac{3}{(i+1)\big((i+1)^2+4\big)} &\le \dfrac{1}{20}\\[5pt] 60 &\le (i+1)\big((i+1)^2+4\big)\\[5pt] 60 &\le (i+1)\big(i^2+2i+1+4\big)\\[5pt] 60 &\le (i+1)\big(i^2+2i+5\big)\\[5pt] 60 &\le i^3+3i^2+7i+5\\[5pt] i^3+3i^2+7i+5 & \ge \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{60}. \end{align*}

example.title: Determining the Values of N Such That the Error in the Nth Partial Sum Is Smaller Than a Given Number

question.text:
Given that
\[
S = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{n = 1}^\infty  {\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^{n+1}}}}{{\sqrt{n+1} }}}
\]
and that $s_i$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine the values of $i$ such that $|S-s_i| < 0.01.$
question.explanation:
First, let $a_n =\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}}$ and $b_n=\dfrac{( - 1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n+1}}.$ Then $a_n$ is decreasing for $n \geq 1$ and $a_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty.$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

\[ |S-s_i| < |b_{i+1}|. \]

So, we require

\begin{align*} \left|\dfrac{( - 1)^{i+2}}{\sqrt{(i+1)+1}}\right| &\leq 0.01\\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{i+2}} & \leq \dfrac{1}{100}\\[5pt] \sqrt[2]{i+2} & \geq 100\\[5pt] (i+2)^{1/2} & \geq 100\\[5pt] i+2 & \geq (100)^{2}\\[5pt] i+2 & \geq 10000\\[5pt] i & \geq \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{9998}. \end{align*}

example.title: Determining the Values of N Such That the Error in the Nth Partial Sum Is Smaller Than a Given Number

question.text:
Given that
\[
S = \displaystyle \sum_{n=3}^\infty {\dfrac{{{{2( - 1)}^n}}}{{\ln (2n+1)}}}
\]
and that $s_i$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S - s_i| <          0.2.$
question.explanation:
First, let $a_n =\dfrac{2}{\ln (2n+1)}$ and $b_n={\dfrac{{{{( - 1)}^n\, 2}}}{{\ln (2n+1)}}}.$ Then $a_n$ is decreasing for $n \geq 3$ and $a_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty.$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that \[ |S - s_i| < |b_{i + 1}|. \]

So, we require

\begin{align*} |b_{i + 1}|=\left|\dfrac{(-1)^{i+1}\, 2}{\ln(2(i+1)+1)}\right| &\leq 0.2\\[5pt] \dfrac{2}{\ln(2i+3)} &\leq 0.2\\[5pt] \dfrac{2}{\ln(2i+3)} &\leq \dfrac{1}{5}\\[5pt] 10 &\leq \ln(2i+3)\\[5pt] \ln(2i+3) & \geq \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{10}. \end{align*}
